definition: Having no particular interest in or concern about something.
example: The cat seemed indifferent to the new toy and went back to sleep on the windowsill.
nuance: Indifferent means not caring either way; disinterested, often confused with it, strictly means impartial, with no personal stake.
prompt: A student hears that her school will switch from blue uniforms to green ones next fall.
options: Mara was indifferent to the switch; either color suited her fine.
Mara was indifferent to the change, so she wrote three angry letters to the principal begging them to reconsider.
Mara looked indifferent from her classmates once she put on the new green uniform.
Mara was indifferent, torn between her love of green and her loyalty to the old blue.
reasons: Not minding which outcome happens is exactly what this lack of concern looks like.
Angry letters and begging show strong feelings, the reverse of not caring.
This confuses the word with different; it describes attitude, not appearance.
Being torn by strong pulls on both sides is ambivalence, not an absence of feeling.

practice.prompt: A chef asks a diner whether he would like rice or potatoes with his meal.
options: Theo was indifferent and refused to eat unless the chef served potatoes, nothing else.
Theo chose rice because it tasted indifferent from the potatoes he had last week.
Theo answered in an indifferent voice that was full of warmth and excitement.
Theo was indifferent, so he told the chef to bring whichever side was easier.
reasons: Insisting on one option reveals a firm preference, which contradicts not caring.
This treats the word as a form of different; it cannot mean unlike something else.
A warm, excited tone signals real interest, which clashes with a flat, uncaring one.
Letting someone else pick because no choice matters to you shows a lack of preference.
